title: Module 3 · Information Systems Infrastructure and Cloud Services
description: Interactive module on the information systems infrastructure: computer hardware and the six classes of computer, system software and operating systems, storage and data types, computer networks, the internet and the World Wide Web, intranets and extranets, data centers, obsolescence and other drivers of infrastructure change, and cloud computing including the five characteristics, IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, with supplements on database technology and on business uses of the internet.
hero:
Module 3

Information Systems Infrastructure and Cloud Services

Module 1 asked what an information system is. Module 2 asked which system a company should build and why. This module asks the question underneath both of those: what does all of it actually run on, and who pays for it. Every app you have ever used is a program on a machine, in a room, reachable over a wire. A manager who cannot name those parts cannot judge a proposal about them — and cannot tell the difference between a bill that is large because the work is large and a bill that is large because nobody was watching.

How to use this page

  1. Assume no background. Every part is explained in ordinary language before anything uses it. If you have never opened a computer or thought about where a website lives, this page was written for you and nothing here assumes otherwise.
  2. Answer as you go. The activities sit inside the reading, at the point where the reading has just earned them. When you answer a question, every option explains itself — including the three you did not pick, because knowing why a wrong answer is wrong is the part that transfers.
  3. Watch for the two supplements. The last two sections are labeled application supplements. They are not textbook objectives; they connect this chapter’s material to the database work the course does elsewhere and to the way businesses actually use the internet.
  4. Retry anything. Restart one activity, one section, or the whole page. Your best result stays in this browser until you clear it; answers reset on reload so every attempt is fresh.
  5. Finish with the final challenge. Situations rather than definitions, scored by objective, so a weak area shows up instead of being averaged away.

Where this module sits in the course objectives

The three modules are organized around the textbook’s own learning objectives, but the course is graded against a different list. This table says plainly which of the eleven course objectives this module serves, and which ones it does not, so you always know why you are reading something.

Course objectiveWhat this module does with it
4. Apply a working knowledge of computer hardware, software, database technology and computer networks This module’s main job. Hardware, system software and storage, networks, and the internet and the web are four full sections; the database half is picked up in the supplement on databases and SQLite.
5. Delineate how businesses use internet technology for electronic commerce, communicating with employees and working with business partners Also central. The web section explains how the internet carries anything at all; the section on intranets, extranets and data centers covers employees and partners directly; the last supplement puts all three uses side by side.
1. Describe what a company’s information systems department does Supporting. Obtaining, running, upgrading and eventually renting the infrastructure is a large part of that department’s work, and the sections on managerial issues and on choosing a provider are about those decisions.
2. Discuss how companies use information systems to manage internal operations and make decisions Supporting. Transaction processing, operational and archival data, and the extranet that gives management real-time information all appear here as the plumbing under Module 2’s decisions.
3. Discuss how companies use information technology for competitive advantage by changing their marketplace Supporting. Renting the commodity so you can build the thing that makes you different is the same argument Module 2 made about strategy, applied to plumbing — and several firms in this chapter sell the infrastructure they had to build anyway.
8. Describe the individual and organizational consequences of the use of information technology Supporting. Energy and cooling, electronic waste and equipment disposal, personal devices arriving at work, and data protection rules deciding where a company’s data may physically sit.
9. Recognize security breaches and computer crimes Supporting. A stolen credential that produced a ruinous bill, encrypted versus unencrypted web traffic, firewalls and private tunnels, vehicles as computers on wheels, and who can audit your data once it is not in your building.
6. Outline the life cycle of an information system · 7. Recognize a business problem solvable with technology, then work with the information systems team on a solution Not taught here. Objective 7’s first half — spotting the problem and saying what kind of system it needs — is practised in Modules 1 and 2.

Parts

What it is made of

Machines, the software that drives them, somewhere to keep the data, and wires between them. Five components, and every system you use is some arrangement of them.

Reach

How it connects

A network is three things: something to say, a path, and an agreed way of saying it. The internet and the web are that idea at world scale.

Decay

Why it never stays finished

Hardware ages, software stops being supported, data piles up, demand spikes in December, and the electricity bill grows. Owning is a running cost, not a purchase.

Rent

Why so much of it is rented

Somebody else owns the building, the power and the cooling, and you pay for what you use. That changes the economics, the risks and the questions you have to ask.

One idea connects the whole module Infrastructure is the part of technology a business would rather not think about, and that is exactly why it decides so much. What you can build, how fast you can try it, what it costs you when nobody uses it and what it costs you when everybody does — all of that is settled by the plumbing long before anyone writes a strategy about it.

Reference

Chapter vocabulary

Every term the chapter defines, in one place, written so it makes sense on its own with an example beside it. Search by word, or filter by the objective the term belongs to. This chapter has more vocabulary than the two before it, and a good deal of the difficulty is pairs of terms that sound almost the same and mean genuinely different things — the deep web and the dark web, an intranet and an extranet, grid computing and cloud computing, a client and a server. Use this while you read rather than after.
finalIntro:
Put it together

Final challenge

Situations rather than definitions. Each one describes something happening in an organization and asks what is actually going on, which is the form this material takes once you are the person being asked. Every company described is invented. Answer all of them, then score: the result breaks out by objective, so a weak area points at the section to reread instead of disappearing into a single number.
foot: What to do next. Take one service you use every day and trace it all the way down. Where does the data sit? Whose machines are they, and in whose building? What has to be working for the thing to load — the wire, the address, the server, the power, the cooling? Then ask the two questions this module keeps returning to: what would this cost to own, and what would it cost the business on the day it is not available. Being able to answer those two about something ordinary is what it means to have a working knowledge of an infrastructure.
